episodes.text: Progressed without interruption through the Ottoman Empire's most selective military-education track (Selanik military secondary school, Manastır military high school, the Harbiye War College, then the War Academy), completing each stage before advancing to the next.

As a junior officer posted to Damascus in 1905, co-founded a small, secret society of reform-minded officers ('Vatan ve Hurriyet') opposed to the autocratic rule of the sultan, organizing collective opposition through a deliberately secret, multi-member structure rather than acting alone.

In 1911-12 volunteered for combat service in the Italo-Turkish War in Ottoman Libya, a theater the Ottoman government had already left chronically under-resourced (roughly 8,000 Ottoman troops plus allied irregulars against a 150,000-strong Italian invasion force), rather than a more secure posting.

Commanded Ottoman forces at Tobruk and Derna in Libya despite severe material disadvantage, winning the 22 December 1911 Battle of Tobruk; during the 16-17 January 1912 Battle of Derna, personally engaged in an assault on an Italian-held fortress and was struck by rubble from an aerial bombardment.

At Gallipoli on 25 April 1915, before his own full regiment had arrived, personally identified the strategic high ground the landing forces were moving toward and ordered troops present to engage immediately regardless, telling the outnumbered 57th Regiment: 'I do not order you to attack, I order you to die.' Most of the regiment died in the resulting engagement, but the assault held the ridge.

On 10 August 1915 at Chunuk Bayiri, shrapnel struck his chest directly over his pocket watch, shattering it but sparing him serious injury; when an aide cried out in horror believing him hit, he covered the aide's mouth with his own hand and replied 'No such thing!', suppressing the report of his own injury in the moment.

Biographical treatment credits his Gallipoli performance to an 'uncanny ability to predict where the attack would occur,' likening his anticipatory reasoning under uncertainty to a chess player's, and frames his broader early-career pattern as one of actively seizing openings for advancement rather than passively waiting for recognition.

In May 1919, used an official Ottoman government assignment to disarm and demobilize remaining Anatolian forces per Allied demands as the platform to instead begin organizing national resistance to the occupation -- the opposite of the assignment's actual purpose.

After the Ottoman government stripped him of his official military position on 23 June 1919, resigned all remaining Ottoman functions entirely on 8 July 1919 and declared himself a private individual -- accepting total loss of institutional legitimacy and formal authority rather than stand down, then continued organizing resistance anyway.

In August-September 1921 at the Battle of the Sakarya, with Greek forces advancing to within 80km of Ankara, personally assumed direct field command and rejected a static-defensive-line strategy, ordering total territory-wide resistance instead: 'There is no line of defense, there is a field of defense, and this field is the entire homeland.'

Delegated the critical, high-visibility Mudanya Armistice and Lausanne Peace Conference negotiations entirely to a single trusted subordinate, Ismet (Inonu), rather than conducting them personally, while retaining ultimate political direction and backing -- the negotiations secured most of the Nationalists' core demands.

Accepted and implemented, as the new state's political leader, the Lausanne settlement's compulsory Greek-Turkish population exchange affecting at least 1.6 million people -- a defining, civilian-affecting feature of the peace settlement rather than a purely military or diplomatic one.

Proposed abolishing the Sultanate on 1 November 1922, timed specifically three days after the Sultan's government attempted to send its own delegation to the postwar peace talks -- treating that act as an unacceptable claim to continued relevance by the old dynasty and moving immediately in response.

Deliberately delayed abolishing the still-standing Caliphate outright in 1923 despite personal ideological opposition to it, per scholarly analysis specifically because it 'still commanded a considerable degree of support from the common people,' instead spending January-March 1923 personally touring Anatolia to build direct public support before acting.

In advance of the 1924 Caliphate abolition, pre-organized a specific loyal inner circle (Ismet Inonu, Fevzi Cakmak, Kazim Ozalp) to counter anticipated resistance from other senior former comrades-in-arms (Rauf, Refet), and separately secured passage of a GNA law threatening treason prosecution for anyone who opposed the coming legislation.

Publicly justified the coming Caliphate abolition using Islamic-modernist arguments (that early Islam featured 'consultative government' compatible with national-assembly authority) even while simultaneously moving the state toward much more thoroughgoing secularism than that argument implied, later stating outright that 'religion is only a matter of the conscience of the individual' -- a tension scholarly analysis explicitly flags as real, not merely a later observer's judgment.

In early 1924, treated two specific developments (international Muslim leaders' supportive letters reaching the Caliph; a former close ally's visit to the Caliph) as the decisive trigger to abolish the Caliphate immediately rather than continue delaying, formally abolishing it by GNA decree on 3 March 1924 and exiling over 230 members of the Ottoman dynasty the same week.

Within roughly a year of the Republic's 1923 proclamation, several of his own closest wartime collaborators and co-signatories of the founding congresses (Karabekir, Cebesoy, Refet, Orbay, Adivar) founded an opposition party (17 November 1924), motivated partly by their own loss of influence and disagreement with the pace of one-party rule -- his own founding-generation inner circle splitting into open political opposition against him.

Following the February-March 1925 Sheikh Said Rebellion, the government (under PM Inonu, with Mustafa Kemal as president overseeing) enacted the 4 March 1925 Law on the Maintenance of Order, curtailing press freedom and authorizing closure of opposition organizations; using the rebellion as proximate justification, closed the Progressive Republican Party entirely on 5 June 1925, eliminating the country's only organized opposition roughly seven months after its founding.

The Independence Tribunals established under the Law on the Maintenance of Order prosecuted several thousand people in the Sheikh Said Rebellion's wake; Sheikh Said and 47 followers were sentenced to death on 28-29 June 1925 and hanged publicly the next day in Diyarbakir -- a mass execution carried out within days of sentencing.

On 25 August 1925, toured the religiously conservative town of Kastamonu and personally presented Western-style hats to its conservative notables in person, opening with the deliberately blunt statement 'This, gentlemen, is called a hat' -- introducing a symbolically loaded reform through direct personal demonstration in the most resistant possible setting, and was met with cold, silent reception.

The Hat Law provoked genuine spontaneous armed unrest in several regions (Erzurum, Kayseri, Guneysu); Independence Tribunals sentenced 57 hat-law resisters to death, including religious scholar Iskilipli Atif Hoca, author of a widely circulated anti-hat-reform pamphlet, specifically targeted as a chief provocateur.

In 1928, when his own Language Council proposed a cautious five-to-fifteen-year gradual transition to the new Latin alphabet, personally overruled this timeline outright, stating the change would happen 'either in three months, or not at all,' reasoning that a slow transition would mean people never bothered learning the new script at all.

Personally toured the country for months (August-November 1928) with a portable blackboard and chalk, giving writing lessons himself in schools and village squares under the adopted title 'Head Teacher,' and publicly unveiled the new alphabet in Istanbul on 9 August 1928 by personally demonstrating the new letters on a blackboard rather than delegating the demonstration.

After judging that the alphabet reform's accompanying Turkish-purification push had overshot his intent, producing an impoverished vocabulary, privately complained to Prime Minister Inonu, 'We can't speak, we've been left without a tongue, we've worked this hard and brought out a small pocketbook,' then endorsed the since-discredited 'Sun-Language Theory' as a face-saving justification for reintroducing stripped-out vocabulary rather than a simple reversal.

Championed a reform program that granted Turkish women full national suffrage on 5 December 1934 (local suffrage already granted 1930) -- earlier than several Western European democracies of the same era -- and 18 women were elected to the GNA in the first election in which women participated (8 February 1935).

Deliberately drew his 1926 legal-code reform across multiple different foreign legal traditions rather than adopting any single national model wholesale -- German commercial law, Italian criminal law, and Swiss civil law -- with the new civil code specifically abolishing sharia-based family law, ending legal polygamy, and establishing equal inheritance rights.

Following his 1923 marriage to Latife Hanim, a prior romantic relationship (Fikriye Hanim, a maternal-side relative who had lived at the presidential residence) ended in her death by gunshot outside the residence on 21 May 1924, nine days before her death on 31 May 1924; he is documented as having been deeply troubled by her death, and the precise circumstances remained disputed even in a re-investigation roughly ninety years later.

When his mother Zubeyde Hanim died in January 1923, was documented as deeply affected, giving an unusually emotional, tearful speech at her graveside during his first visit to it in front of senior military colleagues, with contemporaneous accounts specifically noting his distress at not having been able to properly care for her during the years he devoted to the national movement.

Divorced Latife Hanim in July-August 1925 via a unilateral divorce executed under the older Islamic legal convention (a brief two-line declaration), notably before the new, more equitable civil-code divorce procedures he himself had championed had actually come into force -- using the older, less equitable mechanism for his own personal divorce even while abolishing it for the wider population.

In 1925, when a twelve-year-old girl (Sabiha, later Gokcen) approached him directly during a visit to Bursa asking for placement in a boarding school, he was moved by her circumstances, personally sought her brother's permission, and brought her into his own household rather than merely arranging external schooling -- the first of several children he went on to adopt.

A 1926 assassination plot against him was uncovered in advance via a telegram, prompting him to postpone a planned Izmir visit; the lead conspirator, a former GNA delegate who had fallen out with him politically, is documented via contemporaneous London Times reporting as having 'admitted at the outset his intention to kill the President of the Republic' once arrested.

The subsequent 1926 Independence Tribunal investigation expanded well beyond the immediate plotters to implicate a wider network of former political opponents; 15 people were sentenced to death (exceeding the 11 the prosecutor had requested) and hanged the next day, and the plot's aftermath is explicitly characterized as having licensed a broader purge that dismantled remaining organized opposition and left him in essentially unchallenged control for the rest of his life.

Maintained a documented, quantified daily pattern across his presidency of 10-15 cups of coffee, 30-40 (up to 50) cigarettes, an unbalanced diet, and work sessions sometimes exceeding 30 hours without rest, contributing (per a cardiology-journal retrospective) to at least five documented coronary episodes between 1923 and 1927.

The most severe of his documented coronary episodes occurred 22-23 May 1927, specifically while he was in the midst of preparing his 36.5-hour Nutuk address, with severe chest pain radiating to the left arm, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea, and distress at rest.

Rather than suppress or resent foreign press coverage of his own heavy drinking, was documented as pleased by it, reasoning 'If they didn't write these things, the people wouldn't understand me'; when a French journalist joked that Turkey was governed by 'one drunk, one deaf man, and three hundred deafened men,' he corrected him rather than take offense: 'Turkey is governed by only one drunk.'

His private late-night gatherings (raki-table discussions with close colleagues, sometimes running until dawn, doubling as an informal policy-discussion venue) periodically became genuinely volatile -- documented instances of raised voices, brandished revolvers, and slapped faces among his drinking companions, requiring more sober members of the group to intervene and de-escalate.

Across 15-20 October 1927, personally delivered the Nutuk -- a single continuous 36-hour-33-minute address across six days covering the entire 1919-1927 founding period in his own words and sequence of events -- to his own party congress and foreign press, at a point when several participants in the founding period had become his political opponents; scholarly treatment analyzes it as an act of defining the official historical view of the Republic's founding.

Through 1937 showed visible signs of declining health; a 1938 trip to Yalova was disrupted by acute illness, and on returning to Ankara he was advised to travel to Istanbul, where he was diagnosed with cirrhosis of the liver, with documented symptoms including persistent nosebleeds, loss of appetite, and significant itching.

Died 10 November 1938 at 9:05am at Dolmabahce Palace in Istanbul from cirrhosis of the liver, with a cardiology-journal retrospective noting the underlying cause was plausibly multifactorial (heart strain, prior malaria and anti-malarial medication effects) rather than attributable to alcohol alone.
